Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

derivations.claim: If $P^*=P$ and $P^2=P$, then $\mathbb C^N=\operatorname{ran}P\oplus\ker P$: every $x$ equals $Px+(x-Px)$, and the intersection is zero. The two summands are orthogonal because $\langle Pu,y\rangle=\langle u,P^*y\rangle=0$ for $y\in\ker P$. An orthonormal basis adapted to this decomposition makes $P$ diagonal with one $1$ for each basis vector in $\operatorname{ran}P$ and zero otherwise. Trace is invariant under change of basis, so $\operatorname{tr}P=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{ran}P$, while $\|P\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(P^*P)=\operatorname{tr}(P^2)=k$. Thus the stated equations are exactly the orthogonal projections onto $k$-planes, and every such plane has one unique projection.

For fixed $k$, the equations $P^*=P$, $P^2=P$, and $\operatorname{tr}P=k$ are closed conditions on the real and imaginary matrix entries, and step 1.1 bounds the Frobenius norm by $\sqrt{k}$. Since $2N^2\ge1$, [F1] makes $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,N)$ compact. There are finitely many indices $k$; restricting any open cover of their union to each compact member gives a finite subcover for that member, and the union of these finitely many finite subfamilies is finite. Hence $\mathscr G_N$ is compact.

derivations.claim:
Regard $M_m(\mathbb C)$ as $\mathbb R^{2m^2}$ and the Hermitian matrices as a real vector space of dimension $m^2$. On the open set of invertible matrices, the smooth map $\Theta(Q)=Q^*Q$ has derivative $d\Theta_Q(X)=Q^*X+X^*Q$. At a unitary $Q$, every Hermitian $H$ is the derivative value for $X=\tfrac12 QH$. Thus $I_m$ is a regular value and [F2] makes $U(m)=\Theta^{-1}(I_m)$ a manifold of dimension $m^2$. The determinant map $U(m)\to S^1$ is a submersion: at the identity its derivative on a skew-Hermitian tangent matrix $X$ is $\operatorname{tr}X$, which reaches the tangent line $i\mathbb R$ by $X=itI_m/m$, and translation gives surjectivity at every group element. Consequently $SU(m)=\det^{-1}(1)$ has dimension $m^2-1$. The same determinant argument for $(U(k)\times U(N-k))\to S^1$, $(U,V)\mapsto\det U\det V$, shows that
$$H_k=\{\operatorname{diag}(U,V):U\in U(k),\,V\in U(N-k),\,\det U\det V=1\}$$
is a closed Lie subgroup of dimension $k^2+(N-k)^2-1$.

Fix a $k$-plane $V_0$ and its orthogonal complement. A plane transverse to $V_0^\perp$ is the graph of a unique complex-linear map $T:V_0\to V_0^\perp$. The graph projection is
$$
P_T=\begin{pmatrix}I\\T\end{pmatrix}(I+T^*T)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}I&T^*\end{pmatrix},
$$
and its inverse chart is $T=(P_T)_{21}(P_T)_{11}^{-1}$. These formulas are smooth, and such planes form an open neighborhood because invertibility of $(P)_{11}$ is an open matrix condition. Thus the Grassmannian has local charts modeled on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V_0,V_0^\perp)$ and real dimension $2k(N-k)$.

On a sufficiently small graph chart, Gram–Schmidt applied to the columns of $\binom I T$ and $\binom{-T^*}I$ gives a smoothly varying unitary matrix $Q(T)$ carrying $V_0$ to the graph of $T$; all normalization denominators are positive because each list is linearly independent. A unitary matrix preserving a plane also preserves its orthogonal complement. Therefore $g_iV_P=V_P$ exactly when $Q(T)^*g_iQ(T)$ is block diagonal and belongs to $H_k$. The map $$(T,h_1,\ldots,h_r)\longmapsto(Q(T)h_1Q(T)^*,\ldots,Q(T)h_rQ(T)^*,P_T)$$ and its inverse are smooth local coordinates for $I_{k,r}$. Hence $I_{k,r}$ is an embedded submanifold with dimension $2k(N-k)+r\dim H_k$. It is closed because it is the zero set of the continuous matrix equations $g_iP-Pg_i=0$.

Substituting $\dim H_k=k^2+(N-k)^2-1$ gives the displayed dimension. Since $\dim SU(N)=N^2-1$, subtraction from the ambient product dimension gives codimension $r\bigl((N^2-1)-(k^2+(N-k)^2-1)\bigr)=2r\,k(N-k)$. Subtracting $\dim I_{k,r}$ from $\dim SU(N)^r=r(N^2-1)$ instead gives $2(r-1)k(N-k)$, the dimension deficit used when the plane variable is included in the source of a holonomy family.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, let $N\ge2$, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the standard unitary representation of $SU(N)$ on $\mathbb C^N$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas of local sections $(U_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ whose coordinate images are bounded balls, and a subordinate partition of unity with each cutoff compactly supported in its chart. On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology; the calculus lemma verifies that the induced pointwise operation makes it a Hilbert Lie group.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. For a connection form $\omega$, write $A_\alpha=s_\alpha^*\omega$ for its local form. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. The right gauge action is locally $A_\alpha^u:=u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. For smooth $u$, this is the pullback by $\widetilde u$: for $X\in T_xM$, $d(\widetilde u\circ s_\alpha)_xX=d(R_{u_\alpha(x)})_{s_\alpha(x)}\,ds_\alpha(X)+(u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha(X))_P(s_\alpha(x)u_\alpha(x))$, and the connection equivariance and vertical reproduction identities give the displayed formula. For Sobolev $u$, the calculus lemma verifies that the local forms patch under the stated transition rules and define a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Let $N\ge2$. For $1\le k<N$, let $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,N)$ be the set of matrices $P\in M_N(\mathbb C)$ satisfying $P^*=P$, $P^2=P$, and $\operatorname{tr}P=k$, with the topology inherited from $M_N(\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb R^{2N^2}$. The map $P\mapsto\operatorname{ran}P$ identifies this space with the usual Grassmannian of complex $k$-planes in $\mathbb C^N$. The finite union $\mathscr G_N=\bigcup_{1\le k<N}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,N)$ is compact.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is exactly the set of connections whose holonomy action has no common proper nonzero invariant subspace.

For each $V\in\mathscr G_N$, irreducibility supplies a based piecewise-smooth loop $\ell_V$ whose holonomy $g_V=\operatorname{Hol}_A(\ell_V)$ does not preserve $V$. If $P_V$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V$, then $(I-P_V)g_VP_V\ne0$. For each fixed loop $\ell$, the set of $V$ with $(I-P_V)\operatorname{Hol}_A(\ell)P_V\ne0$ is open, since the projector topology and matrix multiplication are continuous. These open sets cover $\mathscr G_N$.

Compactness in [F2] gives a finite subcover, hence finitely many loops $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r$ for which no proper nonzero subspace is invariant under every $g_j=\operatorname{Hol}_A(\ell_j)$. The case $r=0$ cannot cover the nonempty space $\mathscr G_N$, so $r\ge1$.

Define the continuous function
$$h_A(P)=\sum_{j=1}^r\|(I-P)g_jP\|_F$$
on $\mathscr G_N$, where $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm. It is positive at every $P$ by step 2.1. By [F3] it has a minimum $\delta>0$, and $h_A(P)\ge\delta$ for every $P\in\mathscr G_N$.

On each smooth segment of a chosen loop, in a smooth trivialization along that segment, parallel transport satisfies $U'=-B(t)U$, $U(a)=I_N$, where $B:[a,b]\to\mathfrak{su}(N)$ is continuous. Identify $M_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$ by taking real and imaginary parts of all entries. Left multiplication $X\mapsto-B(t)X$ is then a real-linear endomorphism represented by a continuous matrix $C(t)\in M_{2N^2}(\mathbb R)$. Regard the realified transport vector as the first column of a $2N^2\times2N^2$ real matrix with its other columns zero; it satisfies the first-column equation of the square matrix IVP $Y'=C(t)Y$. Thus [F4] gives its unique solution on the entire compact segment, and the same realification applies to a nearby coefficient $B+b$. Since $b(t)\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$, both $B$ and $B+b$ are in $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. For either complex coefficient $B_0\in\{B,B+b\}$ and its solution $Y'=-B_0Y$, $Y(a)=I_N$, skew-Hermiticity gives $(Y^*Y)'=Y^*B_0Y-Y^*B_0Y=0$, and Jacobi's formula gives $(\det Y)'=-\operatorname{tr}(B_0)\det Y=0$. Thus $Y(t)\in SU(N)$. If $\widetilde U$ solves the equation with coefficient $B+b$, put $W=U^{-1}\widetilde U$. Then $W'=-U^{-1}bU\,W$, $W(a)=I_N$, and $W(t)\in SU(N)$. The integral equation and unitary invariance of the Frobenius norm give $\|W(b)-I_N\|_F\le\int_a^b\|b(t)\|_F\,dt$. A $C^1$ perturbation of the connection makes each of the finitely many segment integrals arbitrarily small; finite composition therefore makes all $g_j$ vary continuously in the stated $C^1$ topology. Choose a neighborhood with $\|g_j(A')-g_j(A)\|_F<\delta/(2r)$ for every $j$.

For any orthogonal projection $P$, both $\|P\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\|I-P\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ are at most $1$. Thus $$\left|\|(I-P)\operatorname{Hol}_{A'}(\ell_j)P\|_F-\|(I-P)g_jP\|_F\right|\le\|\operatorname{Hol}_{A'}(\ell_j)-g_j\|_F.$$ Summing over $j$ and using step 4.1 together with the uniform positive margin from step 3.1 gives $h_{A'}(P)>\delta/2$ uniformly in $P$. Hence the same finite tuple has no common invariant proper nonzero subspace for every such $A'$.

A $C^1$ neighborhood on the compact base is specified by finitely many continuous section seminorms; each is continuous in the $C^\infty$ section topology. Therefore the neighborhood in step 4.1 is also a $C^\infty$ neighborhood, and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the $C^\infty$ topology. Step 2.1 gives the finite holonomy witness at $A$.

derivations.claim: If $K=\varnothing$ or $f(K)\subseteq\mathcal A_\infty^*$, the constant homotopy suffices. Let $U=f^{-1}(\mathcal A_\infty^*)$, an open neighborhood of $L$ by [F2]. Choose nested relatively open neighborhoods $U_0,U_1,U_2$ of $L$ in $K$ with $\overline U_0\subset U_1$, $\overline U_1\subset U_2$, and $\overline U_2\subset U$; if $L=\varnothing$ take them empty. The compact family $f(\overline U_2)$ is uniformly stable under a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation: each member has the finite-loop positive margin in [F2], and a finite subcover gives one positive tolerance. Include this $C^1$ norm among the finitely many seminorms in which all forthcoming approximations are to be small.

Fix a small positive tolerance $\delta$ in each of those seminorms. Uniform continuity on compact $K$ gives a radius $\rho>0$ so that $f(s_i)-f(s)$ is smaller than $\delta$ in every selected seminorm when $s,s_i\in K$ and $|s-s_i|<2\rho$. Choose finitely many $s_i\in K$ with the balls $B_\rho(s_i)$ covering $K$. Let $\psi_i$ be nonnegative smooth ambient bumps supported in $B_{2\rho}(s_i)$ and positive on $B_\rho(s_i)$, constructed by translating and rescaling $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))$ on the unit ball and extending by zero. On the open neighborhood $V=\{\sum_i\psi_i>0\}$ of $K$, put $\lambda_i=\psi_i/\sum_j\psi_j$ and $g(s)=A_0+\sum_i\lambda_i(s)(f(s_i)-A_0)$. This is an ambient smooth finite-affine family of smooth connections. For $s\in K$, every contributing sample is within $2\rho$ of $s$, so $p(g(s)-f(s))<\delta$ for each selected seminorm $p$. This construction smooths the parameter dependence directly and simultaneously on the whole polyhedron; it changes no face independently of its cofaces.

Choose a smooth ambient cutoff $0\le\theta\le1$ which is zero on a neighborhood of $\overline U_0$ and one on a neighborhood of the disjoint compact set $K\setminus U_1$. Such a cutoff follows from finitely many ambient bumps separating the two compact sets. Define on $K$ the continuous family $h(s)=f(s)+\theta(s)(g(s)-f(s))$. The straight interpolation from $f$ to $h$ is fixed near $L$ and is $\delta$-small in every selected seminorm. By the uniform $C^1$ margin in step 1.1, choosing $\delta$ small ensures it is irreducible on $\overline U_2$. If $R$ is empty the first interpolation already proves the result. Otherwise choose an ambient open $W$ with compact closure in $V\cap\{\theta=1\}$, containing $R$ and avoiding a neighborhood of $L$, and a smooth cutoff $0\le\chi\le1$ with compact support $T\subset W$, positive on $R$. All subsequent holonomy calculations use the ambient family $g$ on $W$; on the actual parameter subset $K\cap W$ this is exactly $h$.

Choose $r\ge2$ so that $2(r-1)(N-1)>q$, where $q$ is the ambient parameter dimension in step 1.1. In $M\setminus\{m\}\cong\mathbb R^d$ choose $r$ disjoint closed coordinate balls. Their exterior is path connected for $d=3$ or $4$: a polygonal path can be detoured along the connected boundary spheres of the finitely many balls, and a ray outside a large ball reaches $m$. For each ball join its boundary to $m$ through that exterior, enter the ball, run once around a small embedded circle, and return along the entering path. These are based piecewise-smooth loops $\ell_i$. Choose a closed arc on each small circle away from the entering point; it has a tube inside that ball meeting its own loop only on that arc and meeting no other loop. Thus each loop has a private control tube. The entering and returning stems are outside every private tube.

Parametrize each loop as $\ell_i:[0,1]\to M$ and subdivide it into finitely many smooth segments, each lying in a smooth bundle trivialization. Let $U_i(s,t)$ denote transport from the chosen base frame to the point $\ell_i(t)$. On a segment its matrix equation is $U'=-B_i(s,t)U$; by the realification in [F4], left multiplication by $-B_i(s,t)$ is a real $2N^2\times2N^2$ coefficient matrix smooth in the parameter $s\in W$ and segment variable $t$. The realified equation in [F4] applies to the $w$-dependent coefficient $B_i(s,t)+\sum_{j,a}w_{j,a}b_{j,a}(s,t)$ on each loop segment, so $\Psi$ is a smooth real map and its parameter derivative exists. Choose a ball $B\subset\mathbb R^D$ about zero of radius less than $a$ and put $\Phi(s,v)=\Psi(s,\chi(s)v)$ for $s\in W$. Where $\chi(s)>0$, its parameter derivative is $\chi(s)D_w\Psi(s,\chi(s)v)$, still invertible by step 6.1. By [F5], outside a null subset of $B$ the fixed-$v$ map from $W_+\times\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,N)$ is transverse to $I_{k,r}$. Its source dimension is $q+2k(N-k)$, while that incidence manifold has codimension $2r k(N-k)$ by [F3]. Since $k(N-k)\ge N-1$ and $2(r-1)(N-1)>q$, the codimension is strictly larger than the source dimension. there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, let $N\ge2$, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the standard unitary representation of $SU(N)$ on $\mathbb C^N$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas of local sections $(U_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ whose coordinate images are bounded balls, and a subordinate partition of unity with each cutoff compactly supported in its chart. On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology; the calculus lemma verifies that the induced pointwise operation makes it a Hilbert Lie group.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

Assume ZF together with the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be $S^3$ or $S^4$, let $N\ge2$, and let $P\to M$ be any smooth principal right $SU(N)$-bundle. Fix a smooth reference connection $A_0$, a basepoint $m\in M$, and a frame of $P_m$. Equip the affine space $\mathcal A_\infty=A_0+\Omega^1(M;\operatorname{ad}P)$ with its $C^\infty$ section topology, and let $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ be the connections whose based holonomy action on $\mathbb C^N$ has no nonzero proper invariant complex subspace. derivations.claim: The zero connection has parallel transport equal to the identity in the product trivialization, so its based holonomy group is $\{I_N\}$. Since $N\ge2$, every complex line in $\mathbb C^N$ is a nonzero proper subspace invariant under $I_N$. Thus $0\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*$.

The cone $D^{j+1}=CS^j$ identifies all $(0,x)$ to one apex and has boundary parameter $r=1$. The formula $F([r,x])=r f(x)$ is well-defined because it is independent of $x$ at $r=0$, and equals $f(x)$ at $r=1$. For every continuous section seminorm $p$, compactness of $S^j$ gives $C_p=\sup_x p(f(x))<\infty$, so $p(F([r,x]))\le rC_p\to0$ as $r\to0$. Away from the apex, continuity follows from continuity of $f$ and scalar multiplication in the Fréchet vector space. Hence $F$ is a continuous affine filling in $\mathcal A_\infty$.

By step 1.1, the apex value lies outside $\mathcal A_\infty^*$; therefore this explicit extension is not an irreducible filling, regardless of its irreducible boundary values. In particular, convexity of the full affine space does not imply convexity of its irreducible subset.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=S^j$. The lemma fixes the boundary and supplies a homotopic endpoint $\widetilde F:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$. If $x_0\in S^j$ is the based point with $f(x_0)=A$, the maps $x\mapsto\widetilde F((1-t)x+tx_0)$ stay in the disk, remain in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, and fix $x_0$. Their restriction to the boundary is a based nullhomotopy of $f$.

Theorem [F3] supplies such irreducible sphere families, for example the constant family at any irreducible connection, and identifies the conclusion with vanishing of $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$. The example therefore isolates the precise role of relative avoidance: it upgrades a continuous affine filling, which may hit a reducible connection, to an irreducible filling without moving the sphere family.
